### Observed differences

- In the earlier window, activities A01, A03, A13, A14, A17 and A22 were each handled by a broad group of resources whose most frequent members took roughly 5–10 in 100 of the events (led by User_69); in the later window, a largely different group led by User_98 took about 13–20 in 100, while most previously frequent resources held much smaller shares or no longer appear among the most frequent. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007, ASSIGN008]
- A08 and A11 show the same turnover with a separate pool of resources: before, the top resources each took about 12–13 in 100; in the later window, a new group led by User_133 dominates with about 17 in 100. [ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004]
- A04 was previously spread over 29 distinct resources, with the most frequent one handling about 48 in 100 of its events; in the later window, a single resource handled all of its events. [CONC001]
- A09 was executed in about 57 in 100 traces before and about 71 in 100 in the later window; from A05, the share of outgoing transitions to A09 rose from about 57 to 71 in 100, while transitions to A04 fell from about 43 to 29 in 100. [OCC001, DIR001]
- From A16, the share of transitions to A11 fell from about 29 to 12 in 100, while transitions to A07 rose from about 31 to 40 in 100 and to A10 from about 11 to 16 in 100. [DIR002]
- A04 occurred slightly later within traces in the later window (mean relative position about 0.13 before vs 0.15 after; event positions, not clock time). [POS001]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports the hypothesis of a broad change in resource allocation. In the later window, the work on A01, A03, A13, A14, A17 and A22 was handled by a largely new group of resources led by User_98 rather than the earlier group around User_69, the work on A08 and A11 moved to another new group led by User_133, and A04, previously shared across 29 resources, became concentrated on a single resource. The support is direct and consistent: assignment shares measure allocation directly, all nine resource items point the same way with an empirical strength of about 999.5 in 1000 reference comparisons, and the resource family produced nine qualifying items where fewer than 0.01 were expected without a change; the activities also occurred at broadly similar rates in both windows, so the shift concerns which resources executed them rather than how often. Limitations: several activity pairs share identical profiles (A01 with A03, A13 with A14, A08 with A11), so the items are not fully independent, and the evidence cannot distinguish a deliberate reassignment of work from a change in which resources were available or in how the anonymous resource codes map to executors. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007, ASSIGN008, CONC001]

Other differences:

- Control flow shifted as well (four qualifying items against about 0.21 expected without change): A09 ran in about 71 in 100 traces in the later window, up from about 57 in 100, and from A05 the share of transitions to A09 rose from about 57 to 71 in 100 while transitions to A04 fell from about 43 to 29 in 100. Both A04 and A09 are well observed in both windows, so this is consistent with existing alternative paths being taken with different frequencies. [OCC001, DIR001]
- From A16, transitions to A11 fell from about 29 to 12 in 100, while transitions to A07 rose from about 31 to 40 in 100 and to A10 from about 11 to 16 in 100. [DIR002]
- A04 also occurred slightly later within traces (mean relative position about 0.13 before vs 0.15 after; event positions, not clock time). [POS001]
- The evidence cannot show whether these routing and position shifts share an origin with the resource reallocation. [OCC001, DIR001, DIR002, POS001]
